utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-84bis-T, The Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj, Idriz Balaj and Lahi Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have the appearances today, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Daniela Kravetz, Aditya Menon, Priya Gopalan, and our Case Manager, Line Pedersen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence, starting with Mr. Haradinaj's counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Ben Emmerson, for Ramush Haradinaj, together with Rod Dixon, Annie O'Reilly, and Andrew Strong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. For Mr. Balaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Gregor Guy-Smith for Mr. Idriz Balaj, together with Ms. Colleen Rohan and Chad Mair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. And for Mr. Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Richard Harvey for Lahi Brahimaj, assisted by Mr. Luke Boenisch and Ms. Rudina Jasini.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Harvey. Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. If we could please go into private session. There's a matter I wish to raise in relation to the witness who is currently on the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. Yes, Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is Mr. Mehmet Togal and my colleague Mr. Aditya Menon will be leading that witness. Before the witness is brought in, I do wish to raise an issue regarding witness scheduling for this sitting period just so everyone, the parties are informed, as well as the Chamber. Following the testimony of Mr. Togal, we will proceed with Witness 76. The next witness should be Witness 3. Unfortunately, that witness has had some problems arranging his travel documentation in the country where he currently resides and he is not yet here in The Hague. We anticipate if everything goes well he should be arriving this week. I haven't received confirmation of that but that is what we are anticipating so he should be available if everything goes well for testimony next week. But it is unlikely that he will be able -- he won't be here this week to continue after we conclude with Witness 76. So I just wanted to alert the parties and the Chamber to that -- that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are we happy with the wisdom of interposing a witness in the middle of this witness's testimony?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't -- I didn't mean that. I -- we do intend to continue with Witness 77 tomorrow. What I meant is once we conclude with Witness 76, Witness 3 who was the following witness, will not be here if he needs to testify this week. I don't know how long we'll be with Witness 76. But it may happen that we conclude this week and then we won't have a witness to fill until probably sometime next week when Witness 3 arrives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My apologies. Thank you so much for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Sorry I wasn't clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Notwithstanding, do we really need to have a witness in between?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't believe we do. But that's entirely up to the Prosecution. My question is slightly different which is I understand we may have this witness sometime next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Witness 3. As I understand it. For scheduling purposes and because there are some other matters that I know counsel has to attend to, I believe the Chamber may as well, does the Prosecution have any idea of when next week? Are we talking about Monday, are we talking about Wednesday, because there are some other commitments that exist and some planning has to be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're doing our best to speed up the passport procedure in the country where the witness is residing. We are in contact with VWS on that matter. I think we will have further information this afternoon so as soon as we have that information, we will circulate and e-mail to the parties and to the Chamber to inform you. But at present time we're still trying to get some clearance as to when exactly his travel document will be ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I don't know whether the Trial Chamber would think later today would be opportunity just to hear some further thoughts on whether in fact, if there are such difficulties and given the rulings that the Trial Chamber has made since the conclusion of the last session, whether it is it in fact necessary for this witness to attend. If there are difficulties in securing his attendance, the Trial Chamber I think is fully aware that the Defence does not require his attendance, and that the position at the moment -- I appreciate that Your Honours considered the question at the end of the last session. But this is a witness who was called and fully cross-examined on the last occasion. He has given a further witness statement concerning certain limited additional matters which the Defence, as I understand it are prepared to agree without the need for cross-examination. And I did raise the practicalities on the last occasion. But it may be that some thought needs to be given to whether it is really necessary for this witness to be brought here, given the -- nobody is asking for him to be brought here, apart from the Trial Chamber. It's a matter for the Trial Chamber. The Prosecution's position was to have his statement admitted. The Defence is content with that course. And the -- the -- the arrangements now are proving, in practical terms, difficult. And since the Prosecution applied for his witness statement to be -- and testimony to be admitted, under Rule 92 and since the Defence agree with that course, subject to the eliciting only of the additional information which is contained in an additional statement to the Prosecution which is capable of agreement, it may be that all of those difficulties can be obviated. I wonder whether it would be sensible for some thoughts to be given to that today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thought might be given to that. I'm sure thought must have been also given to the matter when the Chamber decided to call the witness, notwithstanding what you have outlined, Mr. Emmerson. As I sit here now without the decision before me, I do not have any clear recollection of the thinking of the Chamber at the time it decided the way it did. And -- but, yes, we'll -- the Chamber will give thought to the matter in the day, and if there's any change you would be advised. If you don't hear from us, it means there's no change.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I just wanted to clarify: It's not that we have difficulties bringing him. It is just simply a travel document needed to be reissued and that's just taking some time. And Your Honours have already considered and rejected Mr. Emmerson's application he is making and this is it at transcript 1119 of the -- of the transcript of these proceedings and, of course, the decision Your Honours issued on the 92 ter motion that we had filed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Just when you thought it was safe to carry on. Just this, if this witness is indeed to be brought, there is outstanding my motion which was filed last Friday -- sorry, on -- yes, submitted last Friday, I think, received on Monday, in relation to various items of disclosure that the Prosecution is on notice of concerning any assistance in any form given to witnesses who may be relocated in other countries. From what -- I've received a blanket refusal for any information from the Prosecution. The Chamber is seized of the motion, at least there is no response from the Prosecution and I don't expect it will be any different from what I have already indicated in the confidential annexes to my motion. But in the event that the Prosecution, as it appears, is now giving assistance to a witness who requires a travel document, that just brings up and heightens the concerns that I have that witnesses are being given at least the impression, that by assisting the Prosecution, they may be helping themselves in their immigration matters. Of course, the Prosecution is under a duty to provide assistance. That isn't the issue. Once the Chamber has ordered a witness to be brought to attend, then, of course, the organs of the Tribunal will do what is necessary to help that witness. But it's -- there are two issues here: One, the help that is given; and, two, the impression that is given in the mind of the witness that they may be helping themselves by helping the Prosecution. I'm sure the Chamber takes my point. I just want to remind the Chamber, if I may respectfully, that I have a motion pending, and there will have to be some decision in relation to that before this witness is called to testify. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait a minute, Mr. Harvey. I'm not quite sure what that last statement is correct. There's a motion before us. It has got to be responded to. There might be a reply and only after then can the Chamber give you a decision. Are you saying do you ask that, pending the decision, all witnesses who are affected by that motion not be called in your motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I need to double-check my motion to see whether I have formally asked for that, and it may be that I will need to formally ask for that. Much depends on the ambit of this witness's testimony. As we stand here, our understanding is that he is only being called to testify to the additional matters that he -- that he provided a further statement to the Prosecution earlier this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As we heard this morning, and in a couple of days before, none of the parties wanted this witness to come for cross-examination. So the parties seem to be quite happy about this witness's testimony. This witness is coming here because the Chamber wants him to come here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, absolutely. But since I don't know what this witness is going to say when he gets here, there may be additional matters that will come out that will require cross-examination. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fair enough. I understand that [Overlapping speakers] ... that I understand. But why -- why should we pend the witness's attendance in court pending your -- pending the decision on your motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I haven't actually asked you to suspend his appearance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's why I'm commenting on what you were saying earlier on which I said didn't think it was absolutely correct because it doesn't stand in your motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You are quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And let me reflect on it. If I do think it appropriate to ask you, then I will formally ask you. I have not asked you, and I will therefore sit down right now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess everybody wants to spend this time in court today. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify one matter in relation to what Mr. Harvey said. He said that we appeared to be giving assistance who requires a travel document. It is, in fact, VWS that's making the arrangements. I believe I said that. And we have been in contact with VWS in relation to those travel arrangements. So -- it's -- that is completely an incorrect statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. And Mr. Harvey did indicate that he is quite aware that the organs of the Tribunal are duty-bound to give assistance to witnesses who are supposed to come here. Thank you so much, Madam Kravetz. I guess there's nothing else from anybody. Mr. Emmerson, you don't have anything to raise. Thank you very much. Mr. Guy-Smith? Nothing. And Mr. Harvey, nothing. Thank you so much. We'll then stand adjourned and come back tomorrow at 9.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think there may be a cross communication. I think we're all expecting to proceed with the evidence today, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, we have -- witness Mehmet Togal is waiting. We believe that he is going to be quite a short witness and we believe that he will complete his evidence today.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I think we may have been speaking at cross-purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed, because I did ask about the wisdom of interposing a witness in the middle of somebody else's testimony and I thought I got the impression that the answer that said, no, it's not going to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, I think the answer that Ms. Kravetz gave you was we are going to proceed, in fact. The suggestion, I think, is now that we go straight ahead with Mr. Togal, deal with him, and then move straight into Witness 76 and we can use the whole day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes. That is the suggestion and next -- tomorrow morning we can start with Witness 77, conclude him, and then continue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you plan to finish two witnesses today, this one and 76.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I do not know if we will be able to finish both witnesses, but at least Mr. Togal I'm pretty confident we will be able to conclude his evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you so much, Madam Kravetz. Call your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The Prosecution calls Mr. Mehmet Togal, and my colleague Mr. Menon will be dealing with that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Menon, good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This witness still at the hotel?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the witness is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. May you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. And good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Togal.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I see that Mr. Togal has the statement that he has given. I don't think he needs it for this purpose so whatever I deal with -- whatever I show him will be brought up in e-court or shown to him in hard copy so if the Court Usher could recover the binder in front of him. Sir, I would ask that after I pose a question to you, that you allow for a slight pause before answering since we're both speaking in English. This will allow the court interpreters time to catch up with the question I'm posing to you. Let me begin, sir, by just asking you to state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: My name is Mehmet Oguz Togal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: 17 January 1968.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And your place of birth, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: Antakya.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And in which country is that, sir, Antakya?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: Hatay province of Turkey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, did you provide a signed statement to the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal on the 10th of December, 2010?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, have you had a chance to review that statement again after you arrived in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, if we could call up on e-court 65 ter 3073. And if we could go to page 4 of that document. Actually, if we can just stay on the cover page for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, is this the statement that you provided on the 10th of December, 2010?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 4 of the document. And, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm not quite -- this first page says date of telephone interview 1st and 2nd of August, 2010. And you're saying the statement was 10th of December, 2010. Do we have a different date somewhere that I'm not seeing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yes, we do, Your Honour. If you were to go to the last page of the statement you will see the date on which the witness signed the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you wish to confirm that as being the date he signed the statement [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, can we go back to the first page then. You see there, it's not -- sir, you see the reference to telephone interview on the 1st and 2nd of August, 2010. Can you confirm for us, sir, that you were, in fact, interviewed via telephone on those dates by a Prosecution investigator?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And if we could go to the last page of the document. Is that your signature on the document in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: It's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Can you confirm for us, sir, again, that you signed this document on the 10th of December, 2010?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I sign it and -- I sign it, and I made it to court, to Prosecution office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If we could now go back to page 4 of the document. Sir, I would just ask that you read paragraph 11(C) in front of you. And once you've done that, just let us know. I don't --

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Have you finished reading that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the Court's permission, I would ask that the witness be shown 65 ter 3003 which is among the documents listed for this particular witness, and I have the hard original version of it. It will make it a little more efficient if the witness sees the hard copy of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is only my computer that is seized? Mine was ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, you have the document in front of you. Can you just confirm for us that the document that you referred to in paragraph 11(C) of your statement is the same document that you have in your hand right now?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: That's 65 ter 30003.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you note for the record -- can you just turn to the front of that document -- the front. What is the eight-digit number on the front of that document, sir. Can you read that out?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And can you open the first page of that document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And in your statement you indicated: "I have noticed on page U0083557 that there is my handwritten name 'M. Oguz Togal' with proper diacritics and dated 19/06/2002."

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: It should be U0083556.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: That's the page on which your name and date appear?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If the Court Usher can just get the document back for me. Beyond those corrections, sir, are there any other corrections which need to be made to the statement you signed on 10th December 2002 [sic]?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: No, everything I stated in the statement is right and correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, if you were asked now with the exceptions of the corrections that you have just made, if you were asked questions about the subject matter in the statement which you signed, would your answers reflect what is contained in that statement?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: Do you want me explain what I wrote in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: No. I just want you to confirm for us whether, if I were to ask you questions about what's contained in your statement, whether your answers would be the same as what is already in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: Yes. It's same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there is a problem with e-court or LiveNote. I don't know if everybody is having that problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's why I had a technician here next to me right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mine is frozen. I'm happy to proceed obviously. I'm not sure how the other parties feel.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mine is active. That is because it is appearing on the central computer screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm carrying on the central computer screen. The other one is [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I'm happy to proceed though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that the witness indicated that he would -- his answers would be the same if he were asked the same questions in relation to the statement which he signed. And on that basis I would seek the admission of this particular statement which is 65 ter 03073.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. 65 ter 3073 is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 03073 shall be assigned Exhibit P302.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And I would seek the admission, as well, of associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I would seek the admission of associated exhibits of 65 ter numbers 3003, 3004, and 3005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have been aware of 3003. What is 3004 and what is 3005?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: 3004 is the search record against documents relating to the -- contains documents relating to the search that was conducted by the witness. It's among the documents that we listed in our 92 ter application as associated exhibits. 3005 is a single document that is actually duplicated within 3004. It's probably redundant to admit 3005, but it was on our application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure, but my problem is that we can only admit things that that witness has looked at and he has looked at 3073 and 3003. In court here, he hasn't identified 3004 and 3005.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: He has identified it in his statement and so the statement is in evidence [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's an annex to the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: The document itself is commented upon by the witness in his statement. I can refer Your Honours to the relevant paragraphs so since the statement itself is in evidence, obviously, his comments on those documents -- on those documents are also a part of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand you -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: That would be a sufficient basis for the admission of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, my microphone is not working so I am speaking a bit louder right now. Apparently, this one is working now. Now it is working. Excellent. I think it might be a bit easier for just for purposes of clarity of the record with regard to 3004 that Mr. Menon go through the process of having Mr. Togal take a look at that particular associated exhibit and confirm or deny his familiarity with the, so we're clear about each and every document that is coming in with this particular witness. Now 3005 I'm not sure what my position is yet because I believe, as he says, it is redundant so it's irrelevant and shouldn't be put in. And I take it that Mr. Menon at this point is not attempting to introduce the document Mr. Togal looked at, which was 3003. Because if he is attempting to do this at this point in time, then there is a pending issue with regard to the admissibility of this document and its probative value based upon this Court's order and decision of the 23rd of August, 2011, paragraph 47, in which the Chamber stated, and I quote: [As read] "At the outset the Chamber takes account of the Appeals Chamber ruling holding that 'the difference context in which the two trials are held mean that evidentiary decisions proper in one case may not be proper in the other. In this situation the proper of inconsistency on an evidentiary point between a trial and a retrial is not unfair.'" This was an issue that we had raised because the previous Trial Chamber had ruled this particular document, and by that I mean, 3003 inadmissible. "The expected evidence of Mehmet Togal who seized the notes in the Accused Balaj's home may cast light on the circumstances surrounding his discovery of the diary. In light of the above, the Chamber will allow hearing the testimony of Mehmet Togal to assist in determining the diary 's probative value and admissibility. The Chamber will defer its decision on the admissibility of the diary and will admit Mehmet Togal's statement into evidence, once Rule 92 ter(A) is complied with. If he is available for cross-examination and attests to the accuracy of his written evidence. The Chamber does not find that doing so after renewed litigation prejudices the accused." His statement is. Diary, as it's been termed, is not. And Mr. Menon knows that. Because he is aware of the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I add a few words, please, if only because the parties were joined on this issue in litigation and submissions were made by both Haradinaj Defence and the Balaj Defence which culminated in the decision of the 23rd of August. Just to remind Your Honours, the background to this issue was a decision of the original Trial Chamber in November 2007, the 30th of November, 2007, paragraph 11, the reason why this document was to be regarded as inadmissible was because there was no evidence as to the handwriting in which it was compiled, and, therefore, authorship. No evidence as to the source of the information substantively contained within it or the way in which the source and the author may have communicated and therefore it was impossible to establish probative value of the substance of the notes. That's obviously not something that Mr. Togal is in a position to assist with at all. So the basis for the original Trial Chamber's decision was that these were notes, the authorship of which was unproven and incapable of being proved, and that the source of the information was unknown. Submissions were made to this Trial Chamber on behalf of both Mr. Balaj and Mr. Haradinaj that the same ruling should follow, not because it was binding but because there was no difference in context between this trial and the previous trial which would justify a different evidentiary ruling. The Appeals Chamber has indicated in the passage that Mr. Guy-Smith just read to you that if the context is different, if there is a different relevance equation, then conflicting evidentiary decisions would say not be unfair. But, of course, the flip side of that coin is, unless the Prosecution can show that the relevance matrix is different in this trial in relation to that document than it was in the last trial, then conflicting rulings would be unfair. The Trial Chamber ruled that the issue of admissibility of the document, the diary, would be deferred, and wished to hear the testimony of Mr. Togal in order to assist in general terms in -- in determining its probative value and admissibility. That's paragraph 47 of this Trial Chamber's decision of the 23rd of August of this year, passage that Mr. Guy-Smith read out to you. In other words, you have deferred determination of admissibility pending the testimony of Mr. Togal. But, of course, Mr. Togal's testimony cannot begin to touch upon the reasons why the original Trial Chamber determined that this was inadmissible and the ruling of the Appeal Chamber is that conflicting decisions on admissibility will be fair if there is a difference relevance matrix. In other words if it is relevant to some different issue. So the suggestion of Mr. Menon that simply by admitting the statement of this witness it produces the exhibit is obviously wrong. But more fundamentally the Trial Chamber is going to have to ask Mr. Menon to explain what is different in this trial that would justify a different evidentiary ruling because what the Appeals Chamber did not say was this Trial Chamber could fairly reach contradictory rulings on the same factual and materiality basis. In other words, what the Appeals Chamber naturally indicated is that if the issues of relevance are different then a different ruling can follow fairly. But if the issues of relevance are the same, then obviously the reverse is true.

utterances.text: Witness 76 describes the circumstances of the abduction and mistreatment of one of her family members in early 1998 at the hands of the KLA. He said that the guards would put him and other prisoners somewhere with water up to the waist. He told the witness that he could hear the screams of other detainees while being beaten. According to the witness, Lahi Brahimaj was in charge of Jabllanice, including the prison. The witness saw Lahi Brahimaj once very close to the prison, when visiting the family member. utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, the witness, I think, has difficulty understanding the distinction and being able to actively make the distinction each time she is asked a question. And this is particularly acute in relation to her family members, and I think the compromise between the open hearing and -- and being in closed session would be when the witness speaks about her family members which relate to her identity, then I would suggest to Your Honours that that be heard in private session so we do not have any further slip-ups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you say she has difficulty making a distinction do you mean -- a distinction between whether we are in or out of private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: That. And also in terms of the information that would identify her family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think it's appropriate for Prosecution counsel to act as mind readers in court for the witness. I will make more clear, with each question to the witness, whether I am asking her a question in open session or in private session, and I think that is appropriate. But if we restrict the entire proceedings to only mentioning -- only being in private session when speaking about a member of her family then, of course, the entire proceedings will be in private. So I will work harder and further with this witness to make sure that we can have as much of this in public as possible, because that is in the public interest and in the Tribunal's interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I further suggest to you, Mr. Harvey, because you can read on the screen whether we are in private session or open session, so in addition to saying to the witness, We are in private session, say to the witness as you ask the question, Please, in your answer don't give me the name or, if -- if there's any identifying feature just say, Don't -- If you go on button that says "video" you will be able to see whether we are in or out of private session. There will be a "PS" when we are in private session, "CS" when we are in closed session. I see you trying to look for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I have a very fine view of myself and yourself on the video, but I'm not seeing the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Because we are in open session. That's why you don't have a "PS" there. But it will come up in red when we are. Over that ICTY logo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I follow you. I'll arrange the rest of my screens accordingly. Unfortunately, my other screen does not show anything, since page 17, line 4, of this morning. So I'm not getting any help from that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not on that screen where you are looking at the transcript. On the other screen. Where you look at your exhibits. Mr. Registrar, we are redacting that little thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: My other screen has now unfrozen, thanks to Mr. Mair's kind assistance. So let's proceed as we can here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: So we are now, I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are at the time where you asked a question and the witness (redacted) who disappeared and you asked for a redaction and then this whole little discussion came about. So if can you remember the question you had asked at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Just waiting for... okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Witness, I believe we are -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: May we now go into open session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into open session. You were talking at the time when Mr. Brahimaj was bringing lots of flour. We are in open session? Okay. Thank you very much, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Witness, you said that Lahi Brahimaj came to bring you flour. Did over people with the name of Brahimaj also come to your house on a number of occasions?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Do you remember who else came?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: Yes. I remember, but he is dead now, and I find it difficult to mention him by name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Well, I don't need to trouble you with that further. Your evidence is that (redacted) who joined the KLA was wounded at one stage; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And do you remember how long he had been gone from your home by the time he was wounded? Was it a matter of two months, three months, one month?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: I don't know. He was at war. I couldn't count the days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And when he was wounded, he was taken good care of by the KLA, was he not?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Do you remember where he was treated?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: In Jabllanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And in what kind of a place was he treated there?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: He was given the first aid in Irzniq, and then he stayed in Jabllanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: So in Irzniq, there was a hospital of some sort; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: Yes. This was what I was told. I wasn't there myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Did you go to Jabllanice to see him while he was recovering there?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: They informed me that he was wounded, and I went to visit him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And the place that you visited him in was not a hospital, was it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: It was a room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: A room in someone's house; yes?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I ask you this, Witness, because in the statement which you gave to the Prosecution, it says in that statement that there was a hospital in Jabllanice where you visited him. But that's not correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Looking at paragraph 16, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: That's right, isn't it? There wasn't a hospital in Jabllanice, was there?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: The wounded stayed there. But they took out the bullet in Irzniq.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. Could we have a redaction, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, would it be possible to proceed in private session when we speak about family members, and, at the end of the witness's evidence, we review the whole transcript and make appropriate redactions so that it may be then opened up to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I certainly oppose that course of action. I do apologise for that last slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. And my problem, Madam Gopalan, is that it does as seem as the entire testimony the entire cross-examination is on family members. And otherwise it means that the entire testimony is going to be in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: But only temporarily, Your Honours. Once a review is done, appropriate portions can then be released to the public. If that is not done, we -- we see that on a number of occasions there have been slip-ups that require redactions and I think the safer course of action would be for it to be heard in private session and the concern that you had about the open trial could be dealt with later on. Because, in any event, if the material is confidential, it will have to be heard in private session anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, Ms. Gopalan clearly completely misperceives half of the purpose of having open sessions. This trial is followed day and daily on television in Kosovo. This witness herself has watched this trial on television in Kosovo. The primary means for the people in the country that are most affected by the testimony that is being given, the primary means for them to know what is being said about these three accused and about their country is by public session, on television, not by reading transcripts that may be redacted or de-redacted at a later stage. And so the suggestion that we do this entire thing in private and then go back and open up the transcript at some later stage does not meet the concerns of a public trial in my submission.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I suggest to you, Madam Gopalan and to everybody, when your opposite member is speaking, please, to take your seat. We don't have a jury; we've got a different ethic here. Are you done? You wanted to say something, Madam Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I wanted to add that is precisely because of the reasons that Mr. Harvey identified, that the trial is being followed closely that we need to be acutely aware of any security concerns and the need to protect the witness. The fact that it is being followed so closely is actually a point in favour of dealing with this in private session because the ultimate remedy is still available, that it is available openly but only at a later stage when we are certain that no security concerns have been breached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But, Madam Gopalan, there is a 30-minute delay in the beaming of the transcript -- the -- what is the English word? Broadcasting of proceedings here, isn't there? There is a 30-minute delay in the broadcast so if we pick up that mistake immediately and redact it, by the time this is broadcast, that problem has been solved.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was wondering about the individuals sitting in the public gallery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, we cannot help those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I note we're almost close to a break as well, and I -- perhaps, we can formulate more cogent responses and come back at that time and discuss this more fully. The issue that is presently at hand that we have been discussing is the question of whether or not we're going to be in private or public session and the importance of the concerns that exist with regard to having a public trial as well as concerns that exist in terms of the issue of the protection of certain witnesses. And I think this is a point that is of great moment to all of us and something that I appreciate that the Chamber is fully not uncognisant of but is troubled by - and I don't mean troubled by in the sense of anything other than it's something of importance to us all with regard to the idea that these trials should be fully apparent, fully open, and fully available to the public with all of the rights of the accused being taken into account as well as the rights of the victim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. You -- yes ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I would just like to add in response to Mr. Harvey and Mr. Gregor Guy-Smith, the Prosecution maintains its position that it has stated earlier on, and we are mindful of the particular security concerns that this witness has, that the Chamber is alerted to, and that's the basis for our position. And my understanding, Your Honours, was in any event that you have already ruled. But if you're minded to reconsider, this is our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Gopalan. Mr. Harvey did ask that we reconsider. And Mr. Guy-Smith suggested that we take a break and come back. So the debate is not closed. So may we take a break and come back at half past 12.00. But before we do that, may we move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought it was Mr. Guy-Smith who suggested that we take the break and continue when we come back, leaving the Chamber with the impression that he wasn't done yet. If he is, however, done, you may stand up, Mr. Harvey. I see he doesn't seem to take -- oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I will defer to Mr. Harvey. I -- I remain terribly concerned about the issue of public trials but based on the representations made by Mr. Harvey, I'll defer to him since he's in the driver's seat right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I may be able to assist everybody if I indicate that that break has given me an opportunity to reconsider the approach that I was originally planning to take with this witness. And, as a result of that, there -- I have been able to identify a number of issues which do not refer to any family members, and which I can therefore deal with perfectly competently and happily in open session. And as soon as I come to any issue of -- any of the few remaining areas concerning familiar members, I will ask to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber is very grateful to you for that, Mr. Harvey. And at some stage, when we don't have a witness on the stage, the Chamber would like, by way of housekeeping, to have a discussion with the parties on this issue because there are other factors that have been brought to the attention of the Chamber by the Court Officers and CMSS which the Chamber would like to share with the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: We remain in your hands, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. We are in open session. May the Chamber please move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Madam Witness, just one matter from before the break. You said that Lahi had brought flour and other matters. It was, in fact, common practice, wasn't it, by the KLA, during the war that they would bring flour, oil, and other food they would distribute to the families of KLA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: Yes. (redacted) was -- took part in the war, and nobody else could bring me those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And the KLA provided that kind of assistance to many families, particularly poor families, who couldn't afford these things for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you some questions now about how you came to make your statement - are you okay with those headphones? Yes? - about --

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: Yes, yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: -- how you came to make your statement in September of 2010. Do you recall how you got to the EULEX headquarters at Camp Bravo when you were -- went to make your statement?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: Yes, I did go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: How did you get there?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: By bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And who contacted you to tell you where you had to go?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: I went there by myself. I couldn't find the place, and then I had to ask people, and then I went to EULEX.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And had anybody contacted you before you went to EULEX or did you go without anyone asking you to?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: I also went to our police station. I went to EULEX in Gjakove. I went everywhere. Nobody paid attention to me. And that's why I went to EULEX.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And was that for the first time you did that in September of 2010?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And did they take a statement from you all in the one day? Or did they tell you to come back another day? How was that done?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: I think it was within one day; however, I'm not sure about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Had you heard information somewhere, on the television, or radio, or somehow, that EULEX were looking for people to give them information?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: I knew it by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And what did you hope to achieve by giving them a statement?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: I went there to find out about (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Very well. Let me just ask you this: Do you go with this as a general statement, madam, that during a war, there is propaganda on all sides? Do you understand what I mean by "propaganda"?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And do you agree that, during a war, there is propaganda made by all sides involved?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And that, during a war, you hear all kinds of rumours that are spread? I -- I'm sorry, I'm not sure if you answered my question or not. Do you agree that all kinds of rumours get [Microphone not activated]?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: What answer can I give?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Well, you can answer this. Did you hear all sorts of rumours during the war?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: About whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Did you hear rumours, for instance, about Jabllanice?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET TOGAL
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I was not interested to listen to those things during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Did you hear -- let me rephrase that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Can we go into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. The matter stands adjourn till 9.00 tomorrow morning, same courtroom. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 29th day of September, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.50 p.m.,
